paragraphs.text: “My sheep,” says the giver of life, “hear my voice and follow me, and I give them eternal life.” What else can one expect from life but life? What else can one hope to receive from light but the rays of light? Or what else can one expect from the fountain of blessings but the goodness of its gifts? For this reason David also says, “From you is the fountain of life, and by the light of your face we see light.” That light is pure and spreads by its nature, sending out many different rays of goodness. For it heals the various ailments of souls and cures the different illnesses of bodies, because he is the creator of bodies and souls. Just as he granted them a single creation, so he also bestows a single healing. And we can learn from today's reading how the fountain of good things possesses goodness in himself.

Jesus came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had turned the water into wine. Remember yesterday's words: what is said in bodily terms must not be understood in bodily terms. Jesus came, not by any movement of the power of his divinity, but by his body's movement from place to place. For if his nature is unbounded in his divinity, then he is everywhere. He appears in the body sometimes here and sometimes there, not by his nature, but in carrying out the order of his dispensation. Jesus came and experienced weariness. He grew tired, not in his divine nature, but in his humanity. “Jesus came,” it says, “and was tired from the journey.” He grew tired in what could grow tired, and not in his divinity, which never experiences weariness. The prophet also bears witness: “The eternal God,” he says, “who formed the ends of the earth, will neither hunger nor grow tired.” Yet here it says that he grew tired and became hungry. “He fasted,” it says, “for forty days and forty nights, and afterward became hungry.” And it is clear that he became hungry when he willed to. You see that the divine nature has no needs, and that according to the dispensation he labors and becomes hungry in the body.

And these are the wonders: he grows tired so that he may give rest to the weary. “Come to me, you who are weary, and I will give you rest.” You see, then, that in his divinity he gives rest to the wearied nature, and according to the dispensation he experiences the needs of humanity. Could he not have made the holy body, which he took from us and clothed himself in for our salvation, travel through the air so that it would not experience weariness? Could he not have done something like what he did when he carried Habakkuk's body from the land of the Palestinians to Babylon in a single moment? Through angelic grace he transported a man, a prophet, from one land to another, and he neither experienced weariness nor felt the toil. And could not the power of God himself have bestowed on his own body what the angel's hand was able to do? But there the urgency of the need demanded speed, for there was no worshiper of God in Babylon to feed him. He saw that the prophet was in distress among the lions because he bore witness to the worship of God, and through the hand of an angel he snatched up the other prophet and carried him there to that prophet. And see the wonders: it does not say that the angel carried him, but that he took him and set him there. See the angel's power. Why are you astonished at the creator of angels? He lifts the prophet and carries him away, not by supporting his feet and raising him up, but by grasping his hair and snatching him away. And we know, brothers, how much the body suffers when someone is dragged by the hair. Yet the prophet crossed so many places and traveled such distances, pulled along by his hair, and suffered nothing. And in a single moment he set him down there, for it was the power of an angel, who not only lifted him but also granted lightness to his body. What was lifted was a body, but what lifted and carried it was a spirit. “He makes his angels spirits,” he says.

And do not be surprised that a light nature lifted a heavy body. To begin with, even here among the created things visible to us, some are heavy by nature, and some are light [?]. And this does not depend on weight or size, but on the nature of the created things, whatever it may be. Why is it that all the great cedars—even if whole forests are cut down and fall into water—do not sink, while a single tiny needle, or a small [?] of iron, cannot be held up by the great sea? Thus this does not depend on size or weight, but on the Creator’s craftsmanship. Yet iron cannot remain on the water by itself alone; rather, supported by something light, it remains on the water and is carried from place to place. They fill great ships with iron and take them wherever they wish. And because wood is light by nature, the light thing carries the heavy thing. Take yet another example: a person cannot swim on the water for many hours, even if he knows how. Since he cannot hold out very long without resting, his arms grow tired, and he is bound to sink.

Just as, under a scorching wind, the root is damaged first, and then the branches dry up along with it, so also in the worship of God: if the heart first becomes blind, then the fruit of the mouth dries up. However much the heretic’s tongue babbles, it becomes increasingly fruitless, as the prophet also says: “The head of Ephraim became diseased, and his root dried up, and he bears no fruit.” Yet often the outward forms of worshiping God can also be seen among the enemies of the worship of God. There is a congregation in the church, and a congregation among the heretics; an altar here, and something called an altar there as well; true priests here, and false priests there as well. Here the gospel is believed, and there the gospel is despised; here the only-begotten Son of God is glorified, and there the only-begotten Son of God is treated as an enemy. Here the Holy Spirit rejoices over the flock, and there the Holy Spirit is grieved by unbelief, for when the Holy Spirit sees ungodliness, he is grieved. For this reason Paul also says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, with whom you were sealed for the day of your redemption.”

And so, when you see the heretic’s religious forms resembling those of the church, do not be deceived by their appearance, but examine the truth. The Egyptian magicians also imitated the deeds of Moses, but these were appearances, not the truth. Moses threw his staff onto the ground, and it became a serpent. The magicians also threw down their staffs, and they became serpents. The appearances were alike, but the truth revealed the distinction between them, for Moses’ staff swallowed their staffs, to show that falsehood is swallowed by truth. And so that you may know, brother, that every heretical opposition that arrays itself in battle against the words of the apostles belongs among those magicians, listen to Paul. Those who wish to live in godliness in Christ Jesus will be persecuted. But evil people and sorcerers will advance in wickedness, being deceived and deceiving others. Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these people also oppose the truth: people whose minds are corrupted, who fail the test of faith.

Pay close attention: he calls the opponents of the word of truth evil people and sorcerers. Why sorcerers? Because they deceive foolish ears, for the words of deceivers are sorcery to those who are deceived. For example, brothers, to those who scratch their ears because they itch, scratching seems pleasant. But when they do it far too often, they cause wounds, and their ears fester from the repeated scratching. In the same way, the words of heretics at first seem soothing to the ears, but afterward they make the organs of perception fester. For this reason the apostle also says that in the last times some will fall away from the faith, following the itching of their own ears. What is this itching of the ears? Being deceived as by myths. Everything the heretics say is myth. For this reason Paul also says that they will turn their ears away from the truth and fall into myths. Into which myths? Those of Arius, Macedonius, Montanus, the Manichaeans, and others like them. For they have all turned aside into myths and oppose the truth. And he spoke not only of their opposition, but also of their falling away. But they will advance no further, for their folly will become plain to everyone, just as the folly of those men did. We have the voice of the apostles as a reliable pledge. The physician of souls is a guarantor with me [?], to dispel [?].

From now on, do not let the outward appearances of heretics deceive you; they revile godliness. For among the Jews too, many had the outward forms of godliness, but there was no zeal for the truth in them. Isaiah compares them to an unwatered garden and a tree full of leaves on which there is no fruit. “They will be,” he says, “like a terebinth stripped of its leaves, and like an unwatered garden.” The congregation of heretics is also an unwatered garden. It is not watered by the water of life, of which the giver of life says, “Whoever believes in me, as the Scriptures say, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” Jesus said this about the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed were going to receive.

See how they are an unwatered garden. He did not say, “Like a garden that knows no water,” but, “Like an unwatered garden.” They say that the Holy Spirit exists, but they do not have him. They preach, but they do not enjoy the gifts of the Spirit, for the Holy Spirit does not dwell in ungrateful souls. As long as godliness is in a person, the Holy Spirit dwells there; and when godliness departs, the Holy Spirit also departs. And we must give a definite judgment: every human spirit receives either the Holy Spirit after grace, or an unclean spirit. I am not saying that the Holy Spirit works prophecy or apostleship in a person, but that if someone has no faith—for faith is a gift of the Spirit—he does not have the Holy Spirit. Even if someone is an insignificant layperson, indeed one of the very least, and has only faith in Christ, the Holy Spirit is in him. No one can call Jesus Lord except by the Holy Spirit. And the soul must either be enlightened by the Holy Spirit or come under the power of unclean spirits. And who would say this? When King Saul acted lawlessly and dared to contemplate the unapproachable mystery, which it was not lawful for him to offer, he who had once slaughtered witches and diviners then took refuge with diviners himself. And what do the Scriptures say? The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an unclean spirit tormented him.

Heretics are a [?] garden, and however many plants they plant, they are not dependable. Whoever follows not that voice but his own thoughts, even if he plants a plant, it is a plant of unbelief. And Isaiah bears witness that anyone who does not have the word of God, even if he plants something, is neither dependable nor faithful. Just as there is a plant of faith, so there is also a plant of unbelief. All the plants of heretics are plants of unbelief, for their thoughts give birth to them. And every right glorification taught by the Gospel and the apostles is a plant of faith and dependable seed. For this reason the Giver of Life also said of the Jews, “Leave them alone. Every plant that my Father has not planted will be uprooted.” And how did the heavenly Father plant? Through prophets and apostles. And how did Satan plant? Through heretics and the ungodly. Let the plant of ungodliness be uprooted, and let no room be found in Satan’s place. Everything that opposes Christ’s power and rises against it is torn down. Darkness that opposes the light is driven away by the light. But let us turn to what lies before us.

The Giver of Life rebuked the cities: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.” Let the Gospel say now as well: “Woe to you, Arius! Woe to you, Macedonius! Woe to you, Eunomius! For if the message preached among you had been preached in Sodom, perhaps they would have marveled at the Savior, glorified their benefactor, and recognized the Creator.” Indeed, brothers, we ought not to be angry with heretics but to mourn over them. And listen to the Scripture that says, “Mourn for the dead for seven days, but for the fool and the ungodly all their days.” And who is the fool and the senseless person? Let David tell us: “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God.’” It is not only the pagan who says, “There is no God,” but they do too. For outwardly they say that God exists, but in practice they do not say that God exists. When the heretic says that Christ is God but does not consider him God by nature, he says it only in words and has denied it in practice. For they say that Christ is God, but not by nature as the Father is, because the Father’s nature is one thing and the Son’s nature another. When someone denies in his heart and mind the honor of the Son’s divinity, even if he calls him God, he does not consider him God, for he destroys the true image of divinity with his corrupting [?].

And now, what is there to say about this? Prophecy was spring, as I said earlier, and the Gospel was the harvest. But do not think strange the words I spoke yesterday: that the time of the prophets was springtime and the season of sowing, and that of the Gospel was summer and the season of harvest. For there are other harvests as well. The prophets sowed, and the apostles reaped after Christ’s coming. Again, God sows, and the angels reap. The apostles became the reapers of the prophets’ seed, and the angels become the reapers of the Giver of Life’s preaching. The prophets sowed knowledge of things to come. They also sowed the coming of Christ, announcing it beforehand as his forerunners. The apostles of Christ reaped. Christ first sowed the hope of the resurrection. The prophets sowed [?] the future coming of the Life-giver as well. Christ also sowed the future resurrection of the dead and his own second coming. That the apostles became the reapers of the first sowing, while the angels will be the reapers of the second, is shown by his own words: “Behold, the sower went out to sow good seed.” The weeds grew up along with it. And, to put it briefly: “At harvest time I will tell the reapers, ‘Gather the weeds separately, and the wheat separately.’” When the disciples asked what the parable meant, he said, “The field is this world, and the one who sowed is the Son of Man.” “The good seed is the children of the kingdom, and the weeds are the children of the evil one. The harvest is the end of the world.”

And it is not without reason that Zechariah reveals the punishments of the reaping hook, which the Greek calls a sickle. “I saw,” he says, “a flying reaping hook. And I said to the angel who was speaking to me, ‘Lord, what is this?’ And he said: ‘These are the curses that go out over the face of the whole earth and consume the liar, his house, and everything belonging to him.’” Why is it not a sword, a spear, or an arrow, but a sickle? Because the sickle is kept for the harvest. The angels are sent as reapers and gather the crop, and there one can see the whole world harvested at once. And from where will they reap? They will draw them out of the graves. They will not cut them to pieces, but will join the severed parts together. Now bodies have been sown in the fields like seeds. As Paul also says, “So it is with the resurrection of the dead: it is sown in corruption and rises without corruption.” And because they were sown in graves, they will be reaped from the graves. “The Son of Man,” he says, “will send his angels, and they will gather his chosen ones from the four winds, from the ends of heaven to the ends of the earth.” You will recognize these words in David: “Gather his holy ones to him.” They will gather them all and bring them together in one place.

All will rise, but some will be placed before the terrible judgment seat as those condemned to punishment, and others will be caught up to meet the Lord as holy ones. Just as, when a king enters, someone condemned to punishment does not dare come into the king’s sight, while the honored and esteemed go out to meet him, so also, when the Son of God comes from heaven and appears, the holy ones are caught up into the heights. Thus it will seem that they are coming with him. Just as those who go out to meet a king and return with him seem to have been with him all along, so also, when the holy ones are caught up to meet the Life-giver, it will seem that they are descending from heaven with him. And who is a witness to this? Paul: “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God. And the dead will rise first; then we who are alive will be caught up in clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord.” See how they go out to meet him and come with him.

And consider this marvelous thing: in this world, those who go to meet kings go in their own chariots and on their own horses, but the Life-giver himself sends heavenly messengers—not chariots and horses, but his own cloud chariots [?]. And why do you marvel that Elijah was taken up in fiery chariots, while the apostles and others, one by one, are taken up in cloud chariots? Do not consider the fiery chariot more honorable than the cloud chariot. Then messengers were sent to the prophet—fiery chariots and fiery horses—and he ascended from these heavenly things to heaven. And like a wheel he rolled from below up to the heights. Then the chariots were rightly fiery, but afterward they were not fiery, but made of clouds [?]. Why? Because at that time the heavenly vessel still had certain earthly needs, so that it might be renewed by the fiery chariots, cast off its earthly weight, and take on the lightness of angels; for from then on he was to dwell with the angels themselves. There the messenger was fiery, and here the messenger is made of clouds. For bodies rise without corruption, and therefore they rise lightly into the cloud. And so that it may not seem that we somehow disparage the former and honor the latter, I said that the prophet was honored with fiery chariots, while those who are caught up to meet Christ ascend on clouds. For clouds are the chariots of the holy God. Listen to David: “He established his upper chambers upon the waters,” he says, “and made the clouds his means of travel.” He honors the saints with his own chariots. Hear [?] Isaiah: “Behold, the Lord is seated upon a light cloud, and he will come to Egypt.” See how he commands that the saints be honored with his own chariots and go up to meet the Giver of life.

And how will they go up? He himself makes it easy. For Paul never speaks on his own authority, as he also says: “You seek proof of Christ, who speaks to you through me.” And what does he say? “We shall be caught up on clouds to meet the Lord in the air.” Thus some are caught up, while others will be stationed before the fearful judgment seat. As the Giver of life himself also says: “Truly I tell you, when the Son of Man comes, if there are two in one bed, one will be taken and the other left. And if two are grinding at one mill, one will be lifted up and the other left.” And the apostles say to him, “Where, Lord?” And the Lord says, “Where the body is, there the eagles will gather.” Why eagles? Because they are to be caught up to the heights. What does this mean: “Two will be in one bed, and one will be taken and the other left; and two will grind at one mill, and one will be lifted up and the other remain”? There is no need here to speak figuratively, saying one thing for another; rather, the interpretation is plain. Scripture calls the ease of this world a bed, and a mill— the severe hardships of those who toil, who stand bewildered as at a mill amid various afflictions, passing from groan to groan and from poverty to poverty. And let Moses testify that Scripture calls severe hardships a mill. He says: “The angel went out and struck the firstborn of the Egyptians, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on the royal throne, to the firstborn of the captive who was at the mill.” For this reason Isaiah also spoke reproachfully to the ruler of the Babylonians: “You said,” he says, “‘I am, and I shall remain forever,’” meaning, “I shall reign forever.” Therefore childlessness will come upon you and overtake you. “Take a mill and grind flour.” For she said, “I shall retain this dominion and kingship forever, and I shall not experience widowhood.” And he brings her down from the royal throne and binds her to the mill. “Take a mill,” he says, “and grind flour; cross the river,” meaning, “You will wander in hardship, stumbling.” And because beds signify rest and the mill signifies toil, the Giver of life makes it clear that both among those who do not toil and among those who live at ease, some will be righteous and some sinners. “Two will be in a bed.” One, who is worthy of the faith, will be lifted up, and the other belongs to the demons. “And two,” he says, “will grind at one mill; one will ascend, and the other remain.” The disciples asked about the same matter, saying, “Lord, where will they be taken up?” He said to them, “Where my body is,” meaning, “Where my coming will be.”

And he rightly said “the body,” because he will appear in the body. Although the body was covered with divinity and permeated by the immortal root, [?] is complete immortality. It did not lose its form; rather, the body's form continues to remain, permeated by and immersed in life. Let us bring forward an example of this. Although it may be obscure and faint, nevertheless, even in something small one can discern at least a few traces of something great. Take iron and plunge it into a fiery furnace. Consider what it was like before it was plunged into the fire: dark in appearance and cold to the touch. After entering the fire, it is bright in appearance and hot when examined. It has not ceased to be iron, but has received something beyond its own nature. Although it has become radiant, it has not departed from its own shape. Whatever shape you plunge into the fire, that same shape appears. Whether it is round, triangular, square, or of any other shape, it does not change its shape. But its color takes on the color of fire. Likewise, the Lord's holy body, worthy of worship, was permeated by the immortal root of the worship of God, and was immersed in life, and is clothed with divinity—not merely on the outside, but, like the iron, both inside and outside. Yet its form continues to remain uncorrupted, to the glory of those who believe and the shame of those who despise it.

Have you not seen how, when people return from a foreign land after a long time, their relatives seek a identifying sign—not of their splendor, even if they return in splendor, but of their former life, to establish whether this really is the same person? They do not examine the clothes as closely as the shape of the eyebrows, the marks on the hands, and the hair—whether it is straight or curly. The body's defects make the unfamiliar person known. For this reason, he does not wish to save the saints through his divinity, but through his bodily form, so that they may look and see that he truly is the one who was not believed by Caiaphas, was condemned by Pilate, and went up onto the cross, so that his appearance may bear witness to the struggle against God, and his glory may reveal the truth. God considered how Peter would leap for joy, and the apostles would dance and move about, saying to one another, “This is our God! This is the one who was once crucified among us! This is the one who was once despised for our sake! Look at his form; pay attention to his eyes!”

And who said this beforehand? Isaiah. “It will happen,” he says, “that in the last days they will say: ‘Behold our God, in whom we hoped.’” “And they will rejoice, and their eyes will see eye to eye when the Lord has mercy on Zion,” meaning that he will appear plainly before their very eyes. The righteous rejoice and recognize their Lord. The ungodly mourn when they recognize the one whom they despised. For if, here in this world, someone has wronged another person and has himself fallen from honor, and sees the person he wronged in a position of authority, he becomes anxious and trembles, lest that person remember what happened and recall the insult. He devises all kinds of ways to calm that person's anger: can he win him over himself, or through friends? But how can you win your Lord over? Through the martyrs whom you slandered, or through the apostles whom you dishonored, whose names you defamed—Matthew and Bartholomew—saying, “What do they have in common with Plato? How do they compare with Aristotle?” Now you despise their names, and then you will go to seek shelter through their intercession—with what eyes, with what boldness? But you do not intend to be persuaded. Will you find strength in flight? Will you not listen to David: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your presence?” And if there is nowhere to flee, O miserable and wretched one, learn to [?] to him as a fugitive. Just as those who realize that they will not escape the punishments imposed by judges according to the just demands of the laws have only one refuge in flight: to appeal to the king and, through royal favor, avert the penalty of their torments. For this reason David too, recognizing the anguish of the sins that tormented him, and that he deserved punishment according to the commands of the laws, flees from everyone and takes refuge in the Lord alone: “You, Lord, are my hope and my refuge.”

Just as the righteous will rejoice when they see Christ, so those who are guilty will be brokenhearted. Even before their punishments, they will collapse and fall at the sight of his holy face, when they see the sign of the crucified one, of which the Life-giver himself said: “Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.” Before Christ appears, the cross comes first with a brilliantly shining light and powerful rays that overwhelm the sun, conceal the moon, and extinguish the stars. First the sign appears, and then the king. Just as here the standards appear first and then the king comes, so there too the shining cross appears first, and then Christ is revealed. For when they see the cross, they will be ashamed that what then seemed hostile now comes from on high with honor. The standard-bearers will be neither the apostles nor the prophets, but archangels and hosts of angels. They will come before the cross and with the cross.

And after saying, “Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven,” what does he say? “Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn.” Severe mourning will come upon the unbelievers, just as great joy will come upon the believers. And it was not only the Life-giver who said this, but before him the prophet Zechariah. “Then the sun will set upon the prophets, and the moon will be darkened. Then they will see the one whom they pierced”—meaning: The one whom they nailed to the cross with nails. “Then the tribes will mourn separately: the families of the house of David separately, and their wives separately; The families of the house of Nathan separately, and their wives separately; every family separately, and their wives separately.” Why does he speak of all the tribes, or why does he mention David and Nathan? Nathan was not one of the patriarchs, but was of David’s family. David had two powerful sons. Although he had many, two were distinguished: Solomon and Nathan. Joseph’s family descends from Nathan, and Mary’s family is from Solomon. Mary was of royal descent, and although Joseph too was of royal descent, he was not descended from Solomon, who took David’s throne, but from Nathan, the king’s brother. And because the disgrace of fighting against God would come upon everyone, and especially upon his relatives, who did not recognize their own Savior, he says: “The family of David will mourn separately.” And because Christ was descended from David according to the flesh, his relatives mourn over what a pledge of salvation they have lost.

And now, so that we may not mourn but may share in the joy and receive the crucified one in glory, let the Jews hear this— Those who put the body of the Son of God on the cross—and the heretics, who despised his divinity. The writings of the prophets and the apostles will be opened before the judgment seat of Christ. Do you think that the prophets will not come to the court, that the Jews will not stand bowed before Christ’s judgment seat, and that the heretics will not stand deeply shaken and brokenhearted at the terrible judgment? The Jews will be asked, “Why did you deny?” The heretics will be asked, “Why did you blaspheme?” And what answer will they be able to give? But perhaps the Jew will say, “I heard from the prophets: ‘I am God, and besides me there is no other God. I am the first, and I am the last.’ We learned this from the prophet Isaiah, and what were we wretched people capable of doing?” And he will say to the heretics, “And why did you blaspheme the Son? Why did you dishonor the glory of the Only-begotten?” Perhaps they too will say, “Peter taught us this way, and Paul instructed us this way: Christ is our peace, who made the two one and reconciled them with the Father, as the mediator between God and human beings. He proclaimed him as a mediator, not as God, and we were deceived.”

Then the companies of prophets will become angry, and the ranks of apostles will be enraged. They will bring out their books. Isaiah will open his book and say: “See, Lord, how a defender of your anointing has appeared. Let the declarations that I spoke about you be read. Let the Jews hear, and let the Christians say whether the apostles proclaimed anything more than I did. Did I not know you, the only-begotten Son of God? Did I not proclaim beforehand, ‘A child has been born to us; a son has been given to us, and his name is called Messenger of the Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Majestic, Prince of Peace, Father of the world to come’? Did I not join together the teaching about your divinity and your saving work? At one time: ‘God, Mighty, Majestic, Prince of Peace’; at another: ‘Behold, the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel,’ which means ‘God with us.’ Did I not also proclaim his sufferings: ‘He was led like a sheep to slaughter, and for the sins of the people he was handed over to death’? Did I not also proclaim his coming? Did I perhaps say, ‘A prophet is coming, and not God’? Just as the prophet Zechariah said, ‘Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes riding on a donkey,’ so I too said, ‘Behold, the Lord comes with power.’ None of the apostles became a herald of you as I did. They proclaimed you together with your flesh and, through ignorance, gave grounds for blasphemy. But I proclaimed your divinity in every way: ‘Messenger of the Great Counsel, God, Mighty, Majestic, Prince of Peace, Father of the world to come.’ None of your apostles said this. I became your herald before the apostles. Let no one slander my book.” Isaiah says this with a fervent spirit, for he is bold and impartial. As the Apostle also says, “Isaiah speaks boldly and says.”

Moses too comes forward, who was dearer and more honorable to the Jews than God. He also steps into their midst and becomes a defender. He begins to say, “Wretched and miserable people!” For Moses has a different manner: he rebukes them calmly. “The man Moses,” it says, “was gentler than all human beings.” “Did I not indeed foretell the fruitlessness of your unbelief? For you could not receive greater things, so I say, ‘The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you from your own people. Listen to him.’ And every person who does not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed. And if you considered this a small matter, did I not proclaim the Trinity at the very beginning of the account of creation, sometimes saying, “God said, ‘Let there be light’”; and sometimes, “Let us make humanity in the likeness of our image and form”; and sometimes, “Come, let us go down and divide their language”? Did I not write with my own hands that the Lord rained fire and sulfur from the Lord upon the people of Sodom and Gomorrah? Would I not grieve over your destruction? But I consider it better to disregard you and not [?] turn against you. And who will bear witness to this statement? The Lord himself, who said to the Jews, “Do you think that I will accuse you before the Father? There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you boast. For if you believed Moses, you would also believe me, because he wrote about me.” And Daniel bears witness that the books will be opened: “I saw the Ancient of Days seated, and his throne was like fire. I saw thrones set in place, and records were opened.” They will say all this to the Jews.

The heretics will be summoned into their midst. Paul will stand forth as their accuser, having been slandered by their godless tongues. They too will be called to account: “Where did you read that the Son is said to be lower than the Father?” They will say, “You and Peter taught it. He said, ‘Exalted at the right hand of God and having received the promise of the Spirit, he poured it out upon us’; and again, ‘Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit.’ ‘God made that Jesus both Lord and Christ.’ And you said, ‘God the Father, who raised him from the dead’; and again, ‘I thank God through Jesus Christ.’ You did not say, ‘[?] him,’ but, ‘I thank God through him.’” Then Paul will open his mouth, which was never closed, for he said, “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians.” And he will rebuke them: “Son of lawlessness, wicked seed, plant of unbelief, did I not proclaim the divinity of the Only-Begotten? Did I not say, ‘Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever’? Did I not say, ‘He did not consider equality with God something to seize, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant’? Did I not say, ‘There is neither barbarian nor savage nor Scythian, but Christ is all and in all’? Did I not say, ‘He is the radiance of glory, the imprint of the divine being, and the image of the invisible God, who sustains all things by his power’?” And they will say, “Did you not proclaim him as a man? Did you not proclaim Christ according to the flesh?” “Although I proclaimed Christ according to the flesh, elsewhere I also said, ‘Even though we knew Christ according to the flesh, from now on we no longer know him in that way.’” Peter too will come forward and say, “You read about my accommodation to the Gentiles and the Jews, but did you not read the great confession I made concerning Christ? For which confession did I receive the keys? Was it because I called Jesus a Nazarene? No, but because I said, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ When I said that he made him Lord and Christ, did I mean when he was begotten of the Father?”

And now, be on your guard, for the books and records will be opened, and the King will sit. The defenders of the truth will come forward, and the accusers will be put to shame. Let us act in time, before the court sits. Before the king sits in judgment, it is possible to win the judge over. Before the court sits, one can appeal; before the fearsome judgment seat, it is impossible to plead. May all of us appear blameless before the judgment seat of Christ, for his are glory and power forever. Amen.
